title: How an interview goes
summary: What Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Atlassian and Flipkart say on their own careers pages about their interview loops and design rounds, plus the companies that have no readable official guidance.

claims.text: The loop has four 55-minute interviews, each with members of its software development community.
Expect at least one question on software systems design.
The online assessment is 90 minutes for two technical questions followed by 20 minutes of Systems Design scenarios.
The path runs from an application to an online assessment, then to a loop that a recruiter arranges once the assessment goes well.
The online assessment also has an 8-minute multiple choice survey on work style, tied to the Leadership Principles.
Different loop interviewers are assigned to evaluate technical areas and areas based on the Leadership Principles.
The loop has five 55-minute interviews.
The technical phone screen is with a senior leader on the team and lasts 60 minutes.
The path runs from an application to a technical phone screening, then to a loop that a recruiter arranges once the screen goes well.
Half of the phone screen covers Leadership Principles questions and the other half covers coding problems and system design.
Different loop interviewers are assigned to evaluate technical areas and areas based on the Leadership Principles.
The initial technical screen decides whether you continue to the full interview cycle, and it is primarily a coding interview with an engineer.
The recruiter says whether the screen is by video chat or in person.
The screen is split into 5 minutes of introductions, 35 minutes of coding and 5 minutes for your questions.
The full interview has a coding interview, a design interview and a behavioral interview.
The coding interview in the full loop is 45 minutes with the same split as the screen, but harder questions and a more exacting evaluation.
The behavioral interview is 45 minutes.
The process usually consists of a recruiter conversation, an initial screening and a full loop interview.
The typical process takes about 2 to 3 months.
For most roles the first step is a call with a recruiter about your background, experience, goals and interest, in which they describe the role and team.
Some roles start with a prescreen form in Career Profile instead.

Hiring usually involves several rounds where you are assessed on technical background and problem-solving, with sample tasks such as writing code, solving algorithms or a case study, depending on the role.
Initial interviews are typically by phone or video, and you meet peers, cross-functional partners and leaders.
The initial tech screen is a 45-minute conversation with an engineer.
The initial tech screen is meant to assess technical skills, and the page points to a downloadable screen guide for preparation.
Later steps vary by role: you may meet potential teammates and cross-functional colleagues, and some roles include coding exercises, a portfolio review or work samples.
The interview is described as a two-way conversation, and the recruiter explains the format and timeline.
The principal guide lists two coding interviews, one system design interview, one leadership craft interview and one values interview.
Timings are 60 minutes each for coding, system design and leadership craft, and 45 minutes for values.
The stages listed are two coding interviews, one system design interview, one management interview and a values interview.
Timings are 60 minutes for system design, 60 minutes for management and 45 minutes for values.
Interviews are scheduled in three stages, and the recruiter says after each stage whether you move on.
Candidates are told to read each email from the coordinator to know which stage they are in and what is expected.
The management interview is 60 minutes with an engineering manager, using scenario-based questions about how you handle aspects of your role in a team.
The values interview is behavioral and checks how your thinking and actions line up with the company values.
A design round, round 2.3, involves discussing and solving a non-trivial design problem.
Phase 1 begins with a 30-minute exploratory discussion with a potential hiring manager once your CV is shortlisted, covering experience, expectations and aspirations.
A 60-minute technical phone screen with a potential peer follows, mainly on past work, role eligibility and a few problem-solving questions.
The phone screen can be skipped or repeated case by case, and the recruiter explains the exact process.
Phase 2 is onsite: 120-minute machine coding, 60-minute problem solving and data structures, the 60-minute design round, 60-minute team fitment and 60-minute culture fitment.
The phases and the first two rounds match the SDE guide: a 30-minute exploratory discussion and a 60-minute technical phone screen.
The exploratory discussion with the hiring manager depends on the case, and the recruiter explains the process.
Onsite rounds are machine coding (120), problem solving (60), low-level design (60), high-level design (60), team fitment (60) and culture fitment (60).

sections.heading: How long a system design round is

claims.text: The loop has four 55-minute interviews. The page gives this length for each loop interview and does not give a length for design alone.
The loop has five 55-minute interviews. The page gives this length for each loop interview and does not give a length for design alone.
The design interview is 45 minutes long and almost never involves coding.
The interviewer typically saves the last five minutes for your questions.
The interview round is called short at 45 minutes. The page does not tie the 45 minutes to system design.
The system design portion of the interview is 60 minutes.
The design round is 60 minutes.
The high-level design round is 60 minutes, with 1 or 2 scenarios that need a fully detailed architectural solution.
System design resources are split into high-level design and low-level design, with a prep video for each.
The design interview comes in two types, systems design and product design, depending on the candidate background.
Every candidate is expected to know basic design principles, and the company tries to pair you with an interviewer of a similar background.
The aim is a conversation in an area slightly familiar to you, on a problem that is unfamiliar.
A product design example is designing an email server, with questions on storing mail as it grows, large mailing lists, spam abuse and reliability under failures.
Another example is designing a client-server API for a rich document editor, including how the client fetches a large document and how formatting appears in responses.
The design round has two types, systems design and object-oriented design, for example designing Twitter or a parking lot.
In object-oriented design you design a real-world problem with design principles and patterns so it stays maintainable and extensible.
Low-level design is a 60-minute round on 1 or 2 real-world, fuzzy problems, drawn on a whiteboard or paper, with no UML knowledge required.
Low-level design expects multiple components, REST or RPC interface design, entity modelling, class diagrams and flow modelling.
Candidates are encouraged to give several approaches, weigh pros and cons and take an opinionated view.
High-level design asks for an architectural diagram on a whiteboard or paper, and may include sequence diagrams for important use cases.

sections.heading: What interviewers say they look for

claims.text: The listed objectives are practicality, accuracy, efficiency, reliability, optimization and scalability.
Interviewers look for the ability to apply what you know to solve problems efficiently and effectively.
The purpose of the design interview is to assess the candidate's ability to solve a non-trivial engineering design problem.
A good solution compares and contrasts different approaches.
The ability to anticipate and work around typical problems is part of the signal.
Part of the signal is whether you have learned to build large systems through hard experience.
A good solution covers both high-level ideas and low-level specifics, moving between goals, approach and detail.
AI-assisted interviews are designed to mirror the real work and assess problem-solving, coding, debugging and collaboration.
Knowledge of distributed systems, SOA and n-tiered software architecture is very important for system design questions.
Resiliency, high availability, auto-scaling, replication, CAP theory and partitioning may all be included.
Candidates should understand what it takes to build or design a new system or platform from scratch.
Technical interviews focus on problem-solving and the skills the role needs, including how you approach problems, adapt to new challenges and think strategically.
Problem solving is judged on how you break down information, put yourself in the customer's shoes and make choices.
The aim is to assess fundamental knowledge, capability and learning potential, and you are not expected to know everything.
Culture is part of the process, with growth mindset, inclusion, collaboration, customer obsession and values named.
The interviewer looks at problem-solving thought process, decision making and operational considerations.
Candidates are told to keep the customer in mind and how the solution might perform and scale.
The design interview is for showing technical depth, breadth and proficiency by designing a solution to an established problem.
Interviewers want to see how you draw on past experience when designing something new.
The guide expects a scalable system with the trade-offs needed to achieve that, and knowledge of different types of data stores and when to choose one over another.
In its general interview tips, the guide says: "We don't necessarily look for absolute solutions." It adds that the interviewers want to know how you approach a problem.
No specific answer is expected in the design round.
Culture fitment has no right or wrong answers and asks for honest answers about past experience, aspirations and strengths.
Team fitment is with a potential team leader or hiring manager and covers motivations, self-awareness, leadership and stakeholder management.
Tech stack selection, scalability of the solution, and choosing between consistency, availability and partition tolerance are listed as separate evaluation pivots.
Tech stack selection covers the choice of data store, web service framework and queue processor.
Knowing open-source technology is not mandatory, and a proprietary component such as CosmosDB is fine if you can explain its access patterns and limitations.
The overall discussion focuses on your ability to positively influence design and architecture.
Start with requirements. The example is how to architect the backend for a messaging system, with questions to ask about how many people, how many messages, latency, storage, and push or pull.
The sample prompt gets vague at first, so the guide suggests turning it into requirements before designing.
Ask clarifying questions about any ambiguities and come up with a plan before implementing a solution.
Start by asking clarifying questions and stating your assumptions, then talk through your approach, including the tools you would use and why.
The guide describes starting with fundamentals and then building in complexity, and asking any clarifying questions upfront.
The problem will be very generic, and candidates are told to start by gathering all the specific requirements from the interviewer.
Gathering requirements is called the most important thing in the design interview.
For object-oriented design, decide the structure of the design before drawing the class diagram.
The interviewer will ask questions related to your design, and you should ask questions to complete and validate your design.
The interviewer asks a very broad design problem and evaluates the solution.
Candidates are asked to make it a conversation, ask clarifying questions, and drive towards a good solution.
There is not enough time to discuss every detail, so find the interesting and hard problems to focus the discussion on.
Outline the high-level approach first, then think about how it breaks down into subparts.
Say which components you would use and how they share responsibility, and describe implementation details with a reason, such as why a pub-sub queue fits.
The last five minutes of the design interview are for your questions to the engineer.
When stuck or without experience in the subject, ask clarifying questions, which shows collaboration and resourcefulness.
Candidates are told to keep communicating with the interviewer as they progress towards a solution.
The round is described as the interviewer and interviewee discussing trade-offs and requirements and coming up with a solution.
The design round is about discussing different approaches at different stages and zeroing in on one.
Candidates are told to make the interview as interactive as possible.
The interview is described as a discussion, not an interrogation.
It is fine to take a few minutes to gather your thoughts, and thinking out loud helps interviewers follow your thinking.
Candidates are asked to be vocal about multiple acceptable solutions, and specifically why they rejected the others.
The page links a guide to interviewing with Bluescape and suggests Livecode for getting used to coding without an IDE.
Most technical interviews require coding and system design white boarding exercises.
The design interview is mostly talking and drawing on a whiteboard.
In the screen, coding happens in a shared online editor, or on a whiteboard if you are in person.
Design interviews are conducted in CoderPad with Mermaid Markdown, with the same AI assistant available as in the coding interview.
Many interviews now include an AI assistant inside the interview environment, and candidates are expected to use it.
The assistant offers several models, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and the company's own, and you choose one during the interview.
No outside AI tools or help are allowed; only the tools inside the interview environment.
The AI-native coding interview supports nine languages, including Python, Java and Go, picked at the start.
In coding interviews you share your own IDE by screen share, and a CodePair environment is available if you cannot set one up.
Zoom is used for screen sharing whether the interview is onsite or remote.
The system design problem is drawn on a whiteboard or paper; on Zoom use paper and pen, the Zoom whiteboard, or share an editor or drawing tool.
Machine coding is on your laptop and problem solving is on paper or a whiteboard.

sections.heading: The other rounds in a loop

claims.text: The coding part expects syntactically correct code, with no pseudocode.
Coding is judged mainly on scalable, robust and well-tested code, so check edge cases and make sure bad input cannot slip through.
A large part of the behavioral conversation is about how you showed the Leadership Principles in past jobs, and brain teasers are not asked.
Each interviewer typically asks two or three behavioral questions about successes or challenges.
The coding objectives listed are efficiency, reliability, robustness, portability, maintainability and readability.
The behavioral part works the same way: two or three questions per interviewer about how you used the Leadership Principles.
Screen questions are short enough to explain in a few minutes and solve in 10 to 30 minutes, and they typically avoid estimation and trick questions.
In the screen, you could solve a problem in any way you choose, and the interviewer could then add further requirements.
The screen covers computer science fundamentals such as algorithms, data structures, recursion and binary trees, and has two coding problems.
The behavioral interview is about your background, what you are passionate about in tech and the impact you want to make.
Beyond technical discussion you may be asked about past experience and how you would approach role-related scenarios.
Coding must be in a language you are strong in, with no pseudocode, in a third-party tool where you can run and compile the code.
Interviewers expect some testing: check the code before calling it done, and consider security, stress, boundaries, error conditions and corner cases.
The listed technical areas include algorithms, data structures, AI and machine learning, data science and computer networking, as examples rather than an exhaustive list.
For algorithms, know at least one n log n sort, preferably two, and explain its complexity.
Each coding interview is capped at 60 minutes and shows coding skills, code quality and conceptual thinking, plus adaptability, handling blockers and communication style.
How you think matters as much as the end result in coding, so communicate with the interviewer throughout.
Testing is called crucial in the coding task, with a recommendation to brush up on testing and TDD.
Because problems rarely have one solution, show other solutions and why yours fits best.
Machine coding has three stages: 15 minutes of pre-coding to clarify the problem, 90 of coding with 1 or 2 interviewer checkpoints, and 15 of demo.
You send your code at the end of coding, and in the demo the interviewer enters several test cases that your program must handle.
The problem solving round has 1 to 3 problems on common data structures and algorithms.
Data structures named are array, linked list, stack, queue, hash map, tree, graph and heap, and algorithm types include sorting, searching, backtracking and dynamic programming.
The senior role adds a technical phone screening with a senior leader before the loop, where the SDE II path goes from the online assessment to the loop.
At this level the third round is a 60-minute leadership craft interview with an engineering manager on projects where you showed engineering leadership.
The leadership craft questions are scenario-based and dig into driving outcomes on large projects, the direction you give teams and your organizational impact through knowledge sharing.
That interview is not meant to go deep on technical architecture. You should still explain why you made architectural choices and how you involved your teams.
The guide asks you to pick complex projects with measurable organizational impact, which need not be your best or most recent.
At the P30 to P50 level the management interview covers four areas: driving outcomes across the software lifecycle, applying and sharing lessons, managing conflict, and taking initiative.
The problem solving round has 2 or 3 problems, close to real-world, to break into sub-problems, with pseudocode asked for some parts and no single expected answer.
That round may ask about the internal implementation of data structures such as queues, heaps, graphs, trees and hash tables.
Machine coding is on a laptop in any language, preferably an object-oriented one with good concurrency libraries, and you can bring your own or use one provided.
Recall specific details of memorable past experiences and include metrics or data where they apply.
Have examples of taking risks, succeeding, failing and growing, and shape answers with the STAR method.
The page links prep videos on system design, high-level design and common candidate questions.
Before studying, ask the recruiting contact which subjects and skills you are most likely to discuss.
The online assessment includes a coding test, and a sample coding challenge can be tried as many times as you like.
Interviewers are not testing whether you memorize every detail of the topics.
The advice is to review computer science fundamentals and practice coding outside an IDE.

The topic list covers programming language, data structures, algorithms, coding, object-oriented design, databases, distributed computing, operating systems, internet topics, and general machine learning and AI.
Keep the customer in mind while reviewing the topics.
The page links a video that works through a system design example and how to approach it.
Prepare a short, interesting description of who you are, where you trained and worked, and your areas of expertise.
Think about complex systems you have designed and what you would change if you did it again.
Practice designing a system the company already runs, from the ground up.
Read engineering blogs about approaches that work and the false starts big companies had along the way.
For the screen, write code in a plain text editor without syntax highlighting or auto-completion, by hand, and under time pressure.
A mock interview with a friend is suggested to simulate the time pressure.
Be able to discuss the big-O complexity of your approaches and review common data structures and traversals.
In the coding interview, think out loud, because the way you solve problems matters as much as having the right answer.
Use the language you know best unless the recruiter says one is required.
Manage time in coding: look for a good solution, but if none appears in reasonable time write a working one and improve it, since some interviews end with no code written.
Be ready to explain your solution, find and fix your own bugs, and ask questions if you are stuck.
For the behavioral interview, review your own resume, be honest about failures, structure answers with STAR and give concrete examples rather than theory.
Come prepared with questions about working as an engineer there.
The page also asks candidates to know the company's six core values.
Review the prep material from the recruiter and in your career profile, and research your interviewers to anticipate their questions.
A practice session in the same tool as the interview is available before it, and practising with AI coding tools and reading and debugging existing code helps.
Prepare questions for the recruiter on team dynamics, role specifics and next steps.
The page says to practice coding a great deal and calls it a critical part of the interview.
If you do not work with distributed systems concepts regularly, review them before the interview.
Research the role, the tech industry and what the company does well, and prepare questions to ask.
Read the job description for the most relevant skills and prepare examples that cover the situation, what you did, the result and what you learned.
Think about how you have used feedback, worked with others and adapted.
Structure answers with STAR plus a reflection step.
The guide lists sample questions under company values, such as handling difficult conversations, advocating for change and putting the customer first.
Coding prep: set up a familiar IDE and test framework, use a debugger if useful, and join Zoom about 10 minutes early.
For the values interview, review the company values and prepare examples of living them in past roles.
Research the company and look up your interviewers on LinkedIn.
Come with questions; if one goes unasked, reach out to the recruiter or coordinator.
For the phone screen, find a quiet place, know your resume, prepare a short introduction and go deeper on any detail asked.
For the first discussion, ask questions to understand the role charter, scope and kind of work.
For design, read engineering blogs on how companies design systems, with the guide naming Netflix TechBlog and High Scalability.
Learn the parts of a distributed system and their trade-offs, and practice a few design problems.
Design topics listed are data stores, distributed systems, CAP theorem, scaling, caches and queues, and Internet and OS basics.
For machine coding, ask clarifying questions, clarify input limits, write test cases and dry run before and after coding.
For problem solving, compute time and space complexity and understand trade-offs between them.
Practice coding on online platforms, since interviews expect bug-free code in a short time.
Learn about the business and the role beforehand, and tell the interviewers something that makes you stand out.
Ask questions, and be honest about past failures, since intent and commitment are valued over success.
Read up on the four values, Audacity, Bias for Action, Customer First and Integrity, and recall times you showed them.
Bring your own laptop if you can, because the IDE or compiler you prefer may not be on the provided one.
Suggested resources include LeetCode, HackerRank, awesome-scalability and High Scalability.
For a remote interview, pick a quiet spot with a good internet connection and phone reception, and headphones leave both hands free.
Speak clearly, and tell the interviewer if you cannot hear them well.
Unless the interview is very early or very late in the day, someone from engineering or recruiting takes you to lunch, which is a chance to ask someone who is not interviewing you.
Interview schedules and prep materials are tailored to the role, and Career Profile shows upcoming interviews, role-specific prep guides and a CoderPad practice environment.
Check your computer and WiFi beforehand, and protect your interview time because it can be hard to reschedule at the last minute.
Accommodations are available for disabilities, long-term and mental health conditions, neurodivergence, sincerely held religious beliefs and pregnancy-related needs.
The recruiter is the contact for questions about the format.
You can apply for more than one role if you meet the minimum qualifications for each, and the careers site holds only one resume per applicant.
If Teams or another virtual platform is not fully accessible for you, you can submit an accessibility request and they will reach out.
You do not need to dress up; wear what is comfortable.
Accommodations can be requested if the virtual platform is not accessible to you.
Ask for accommodations or adjustments if you need them.
The interview outcome is given within 5 business days.
The interview outcome is given within 5 business days.
After each interview you can send that interviewer a personal message through your career profile.
The decision time is hard to estimate, and candidates should tell the recruiter about competing offers or deadlines.
The timeline can shift because of holidays and other factors.
If selected, the recruiter sends an offer letter, and either way you hear back about your application status.
At the end, ask the hiring manager or recruiter when to expect the decision or next steps.
The recruiter follows up on the outcome as soon as a decision is made, and a thank-you email to the recruiter is passed on to the hiring manager and interviewers.
After the management and values stages, feedback goes to a hiring committee, and successful candidates move to team match.
Team match is a call with hiring managers who have open roles, not an interview, and you then have 24 hours to choose after teams are presented.
Open teams depend on business priorities and can change, which is why assessments come first.

noGuidance.note: The how-we-hire interview page returned 200, but its text is drawn by JavaScript. The raw page held only navigation and footer; nothing could be confirmed.

Uber's careers pages and jobs.uber.com returned HTTP 403 or 406 to curl. The one readable Uber page, an engineering blog post from 8 Dec 2015, covers the hiring market and does not cover the design round.
Rubrik's careers page returned 403 to curl, and no other official page was found.
The Netflix Tech Blog interview post returned 403 on netflixtechblog.com and on medium.com. The jobs.netflix.com new-grad page was not read.
No interview process page was found.
The stripe.com/jobs/interview address is a 404, and no candidate-facing system design page was found.
The careers FAQ gives a 60 to 75 minute Craft Assessment but never names system design; it is not used.
